meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: At baseline prior to matching (Table 3S), the GLP-1 RA cohort had a substantially higher proportion of obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin) and higher socioeconomic status (undergraduate and above: 26.07% vs 15.65% in insulin and 11.94% in metformin). In the propensity-score matched sample (Table 1), missing covariate values were retained as explicit 'unspecified' categories (BMI unspecified in 32.49% to 36.08%; education unspecified in 32.30% to 35.89%; age unspecified in 19.74% to 21.93%), preventing true balance of underlying confounding factors and biasing sHR estimates upward (e.g., pancreatitis sHR 2.01, 95% CI 1.24-3.24; renal failure sHR 3.73, 95% CI 2.74-5.08).

findings.title: Incomplete confounding adjustment via 'unspecified' matching categories
findings.mechanism: Propensity score matching treated missing covariate entries as matched 'unspecified' categories rather than imputing or restricting to complete cases, leaving substantial residual confounding within the unspecified strata.
evidence: Table 1 shows unspecified categories after PSM: BMI unspecified in 33.81% (GLP-1) vs 36.08% (insulin) and 32.49% (GLP-1) vs 32.71% (metformin); Age unspecified in 19.74% to 21.93%; Education unspecified in 32.30% to 35.89%.

findings.title: Uncontrolled clinical severity and missing glycemic parameters
findings.mechanism: Baseline diabetes duration and long-term glycemic control were inadequately adjusted due to extreme missingness of laboratory markers, confounding adverse outcome risk by underlying diabetes severity and progression.
evidence: Footnote to Table 1 and Table 3S notes that missing rates for HbA1c were 90.52% in GLP-1 RAs, 91.79% in insulin-only, and 90.45% in metformin-only cohorts (91.27% overall after matching).

findings.title: Baseline paradox: worse starting position, better outcome
findings.mechanism: differential detection bias from higher socioeconomic status and citizen insurance coverage; channeling/confounding by indication (prescribing GLP-1 RAs to patients with higher metabolic or refractory disease); surveillance bias from closer follow-up on injectable newer therapies
evidence: The GLP-1 RA cohort was markedly younger (<30 to 49 years: 41.64% vs 25.68% for metformin; >=70 years: 5.72% vs 8.93%) and had comparable fasting glucose, yet demonstrated markedly elevated risk of renal failure (sHR 3.73), acute nephritis (sHR 3.20), thyroid cancer (sHR 2.25), and leukemia (sHR 15.09).

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Restricting the analytic cohorts to patients maintaining 'predominant' monotherapy throughout the follow-up period excludes patients who switched or intensified treatments due to early side effects or treatment failure, introducing substantial selection and survivor bias that inflates long-term hazard ratios (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Conditioning on post-baseline adherence and treatment continuity
findings.mechanism: Defining cohorts based on treatment duration and exclusivity over the entire follow-up introduces selection bias by conditioning on downstream treatment paths rather than baseline intention-to-treat assignment.
evidence: Methods 2.1: 'GLP-1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months.'

findings.title: Massive exclusion of eligible population due to missing prescription records
findings.mechanism: Over 36% of the initial population was excluded due to missing prescription data, which may be non-random with respect to treatment adherence and healthcare contact.
evidence: Figure 1 and Section 2.1: 362,035 out of 742,437 outpatients (48.8% of post-ID/comorbidity screen) were excluded due to missing prescription data.

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Coadministration of non-antidiabetic co-medications (e.g., antihypertensives, statins, NSAIDs) and subsequent clinical interventions during follow-up were not tracked or adjusted in the survival models.

findings.title: Unmeasured concomitant medications
findings.mechanism: Differential use of nephrotoxic or gastrotoxic co-medications across treatment groups during follow-up could confound organ-specific adverse outcomes such as acute nephritis and gastric ulcers.
evidence: Section 2.2 only extracted baseline hypertension status and demographic covariates; time-varying non-diabetic medications were not accounted for.

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: HbA1c was missing in >90% of all participants across all groups (90.52% to 91.79%), and key demographic variables were missing in 20% to 36% of participants; retaining missing values as matched strata rather than performing valid multiple imputation obscures true baseline imbalances and distorts effect estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Pervasive missingness in primary clinical and biochemical confounders
findings.mechanism: Matching on missingness categories ('unspecified') creates pseudo-balance without addressing the true underlying distribution of biological risk factors.
evidence: Table 1 and Table 3S footnote: HbA1c missing rate was 91.27% after matching (90.52% GLP-1, 91.79% insulin, 90.45% metformin); FPG missing rate was 33.22% after matching; BMI was unspecified in 33.81% (GLP-1) and 36.08% (insulin).

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Outcomes were captured using ICD-10 codes and keyword matching without adjudication. GLP-1 RA users had higher health insurance coverage (75.60% vs 59.60% in insulin and 54.96% in metformin at baseline) and higher outpatient follow-up frequency, leading to surveillance bias and higher detection rates of common or minor conditions (e.g., acne sHR 5.32, 95% CI 2.21-12.81; skin follicular cysts sHR 1.50, 95% CI 1.00-2.24; thyroid dysfunction sHR 1.65, 95% CI 1.07-2.54).

findings.title: Surveillance and detection bias across heterogeneous healthcare users
findings.mechanism: Patients prescribed newer, expensive injectable drugs undergo closer clinical monitoring, laboratory testing, and outpatient visits, inflating diagnosis rates of subclinical or incidental conditions.
evidence: Table 3S: Citizen health insurance was 75.60% in GLP-1 vs 59.60% in insulin and 54.96% in metformin; Undergraduate education was 26.07% in GLP-1 vs 15.65% in insulin and 11.94% in metformin.
Elevated sHRs observed for minor dermatological conditions: Acne (sHR 4.29 vs insulin, sHR 5.32 vs metformin) and Skin follicular cysts (sHR 2.03 vs insulin, sHR 1.50 vs metformin).

findings.title: Outcome definition via unvalidated regex and diagnostic coding
findings.mechanism: Combining ICD-10 codes and text-based regular expressions without blinded medical chart adjudication introduces outcome misclassification.
evidence: Table 2S details regex matches such as '/(acute|chronic)\s+pancreatitis/' and broad ICD ranges (e.g., N00-N01, N03-N06, N08 for acute nephritis; N17-N19 for renal failure).

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: The study tested a large panel of diverse disease endpoints (digestive, renal, thyroid, cutaneous, hematological) across multiple subgroup strata (<12 vs ≥12 months, 4 individual drug agents) without pre-specified trial registry protocol or formal family-wise error rate correction, favoring the reporting and highlighting of statistically significant positive associations (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Multiplicity of tested adverse outcomes without protocol pre-specification
findings.mechanism: Evaluating multiple non-prespecified secondary endpoints increases the likelihood of false-positive associations driven by random variation or selective reporting.
evidence: Table 2S lists 17 distinct adverse outcomes tested across digestive, renal, thyroid, cutaneous, and lymphatic/hematopoietic systems.
Section 4 notes an extreme estimate for leukemia (sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98) based on very small absolute case numbers, which authors acknowledge as potential random bias.

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study exhibits a very high risk of bias stemming from severe missing data in essential confounders (>90% missing HbA1c; >30% missing BMI), handling of missing covariates via matched 'unspecified' categories in propensity score matching, selection bias from defining cohorts conditional on long-term continuous monotherapy, and surveillance bias resulting from differential healthcare access and monitoring among GLP-1 RA recipients. These systemic biases consistently push effect estimates away from the null, threatening the validity of the reported associations between GLP-1 RA use and elevated risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, renal failure, thyroid malignancy, and leukemia.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts and incidence rates per study arm for each specific adverse outcome (only sHRs and CIs are provided in figures/text, preventing calculation of absolute risk differences or NNT/NNH).
Complete baseline glycemic control (HbA1c data missing in 91.27% of matched participants) to assess residual confounding by diabetes severity.
Validated adjudication of outcome events to distinguish true clinical pathology from differential surveillance and diagnostic coding.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure groups based on treatment patterns evaluated over the entirety of follow-up rather than at baseline cohort entry, introducing conditioning on future exposure. Furthermore, the lack of a lag period permits detection of slow-latency outcomes (like thyroid cancer and leukemia) within months of baseline, creating severe protopathic bias that inflates apparent drug harms.
